## Natural setting & history

Schafer State Park is a public recreation area along the Satsop River located midway between Olympia and Aberdeen in the Satsop Hills of Mason County, Washington. The 122-acre (49 ha) state park offers camping, two miles of hiking trails, fishing (especially for steelhead), swimming, birdwatching, interpretive activities, wildlife viewing, and horseshoes. The park's abundance of historic structures led to its inclusion on the National Register of Historic Places in 2010.[^wiki]

Of note:

- Established 1924 on the East Fork Satsop River.[^wiki]
- NRHP listed 2010.[^wiki]
- Architecture by C.C. 'Doc' Palmer.[^wiki]
- Known for steelhead fishing.[^wiki]

# Seaquest State Park

> Adjacent to Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument; views of the volcano

![[heading-seaquest-state-park.jpg]]
*Photo: Chris Light — CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Boardwalk_8753.jpg).*

Seaquest State Park is a ~505-acre park in Cowlitz County on the west shore of Silver Lake near Castle Rock, ~50 miles west of Mount St. Helens via the Spirit Lake Memorial Highway. It hosts the Mount St. Helens Visitor Center; named for Swedish settlers who donated the land in 1945.[^wiki]

Seaquest is a 475-acre, year-round camping park set among lush fir trees in the shadow of the storied Mount. St. Helen's volcano. Seaquest boasts forested campgrounds, great hiking trails and stunning mountain panoramas. The park is connected to the popular Mount St. Helen's Interpretive Center, another worthwhile destination, and Silver Lake by a pedestrian tunnel. Enjoy a boardwalk trail over the wetland where ducks and other wildlife thrive. Seaquest is connected to the Mount St. Helens Interpretive Center by a short pedestrian tunnel. The Interpretive Center features a fun, interactive educational experience focusing on the May 1980 eruption of Mount St. Helens and subsequent regrowth. It also offers visitors a sweeping view of Mount St.[^agency]

# Steamboat Rock State Park

> On Banks Lake in the Grand Coulee area; massive basalt butte

![[heading-steamboat-rock-state-park.jpg]]
*Photo: Unknown — Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:SteamboatRock.jpg).*

Steamboat Rock State Park is a 5,043-acre park near the north end of Banks Lake in the Grand Coulee, named for Steamboat Rock — a basalt butte rising ~800 ft above the lake with a 600+-acre plateau; open year-round.[^wiki]

Amid a Pacific Northwest desert, Steamboat Rock State Parks offers lush green lawns, climbing rocks, boating and water activities, camping and miles of trails for horses and hikers. Steamboat Rock State Park is a 5,043-acre camping park with 50,000 feet of freshwater shoreline at the north end of Banks Lake.[^agency]

## At a glance

- **Managed by:** Washington State Parks
- **Sites:** 213 · **Season:** 04-01 → 09-30
- **Reservations:** Reservable — [Washington State Parks reservations](https://washington.goingtocamp.com/create-booking/results?resourceLocationId=-2147483552)[^resv]
- **Coordinates:** 47.8596, -119.0871
- **Drive from Seattle:** 210 mi · 3 hr 45 min

## Natural setting & history

Steamboat Rock State Park is a 5,043-acre (2,041 ha) public recreation area located near the north end of Banks Lake in the Grand Coulee. The state park takes its name from the landscape's dominating feature, Steamboat Rock, a basalt butte that rises 800 feet (240 m) above the lake which nearly completely surrounds it. The butte's plateau covers more than 600 acres (240 ha) and was used by nomadic Native American tribes and by early settlers. During the last ice age, the monolith stood as an island in the new bed of the Columbia River where it had been diverted by ice dams. Once the dams burst creating massive floods and the Scablands, the Columbia returned to its original course, leaving Steamboat Rock as a prominent feature of the dry Grand Coulee.[^wiki]

Of note:

- Steamboat Rock is a basalt butte ~800 ft above the lake.[^wiki]
- Was an island in the ice-diverted Columbia during the Ice Age.[^wiki]
- Banks Lake created in 1953 by the Grand Coulee project.[^wiki]
- ~50,000 ft of shoreline.[^wiki]

# Sun Lakes-Dry Falls State Park

> Near the world's largest prehistoric waterfall; coulees and lakes

![[heading-sun-lakes-dry-falls-state-park.jpg]]
*Photo: WiiUser23 at English Wikipedia — CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sun_Lakes_State_Park.jpg).*

Sun Lakes-Dry Falls State Park is a 3,774-acre park at the foot of Dry Falls ~3 miles west of Coulee City, at the head of the Lower Grand Coulee among gorges and lakes. Dry Falls is a ~400-ft, 3.5-mile-wide former waterfall once far larger than Niagara.[^wiki]

A high desert adventure awaits you at this sprawling camping park located between Soap Lake and Coulee City. Experience a dramatic landscape of deep gorges and lakes where you can get out on the water, hike and play nine-hole or mini golf. There are 96 standard campsites and 41 full hook up sites that can be reserved in advance. Maximum site length is 65 feet with limited availability. Six restrooms, 12 showers and one dump station are located nearby. All campsites have fire pits but don't have tent pads. One group camp is available for tent camping only and can host up to 75 people. If you're planning to camp during the summer, we highly recommend making reservations.[^agency]

Twenty-Five Mile Creek State Park is a 232-acre park on the west side of Lake Chelan ~15 miles NW of Chelan. A former private resort, it became a state park in 1972, with camping, a marina, and access to the upper reaches of fjord-like Lake Chelan.[^wiki]

Flowing from the mountains to Lake Chelan, Twenty-Five Mile Creek State Park is perfect for a day trip or campout with activities to keep the entire family entertained. Moorage is for campers only. ![[heading-wanapum-recreation-area.jpg]]
*Photo: Williamborg 01:57, 28 April 2008 (UTC) — Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wanapum_Dam_from_West_Shore_-_downstream_10360031.jpg).*

Wanapum Recreation Area is a Washington state park campground on the Columbia's Wanapum Reservoir near the Gorge Amphitheatre. Wanapum Dam, built 1959-1963 downstream of Vantage, impounds Lake Wanapum and is named for the Wanapum people.[^wiki]

The upper loop restroom including the showers will be down until further notice. Maintenance is removing a large blockage that will need to be excavated and repaired. Restrooms are available in the river loop or at the day use. Wanapum Recreation Area is a camping and day-use park in a shrub-steppe landscape next to the Columbia River. Boaters and water sports enthusiasts can unload and have some fun while others can relax and enjoy the water at the swim beach area.[^agency]

## Natural setting & history

Wanapum Dam is a run-of-the-river hydroelectric project located on the Columbia River downstream (south) from Vantage, Washington where Interstate 90 crosses the Columbia from Grant County into Kittitas County. It is owned by the Grant County Public Utility District. Its reservoir is named Lake Wanapum.

The dam, and its lake, are named after the Wanapum Indians. The dam has a rated capacity of 1,185 megawatts and annually generates over 4 million megawatt-hours.[^wiki]

Of note:

- Built 1959-1963 (~$93.3M).[^wiki]
- ~1,185 MW from 10 Kaplan turbines.[^wiki]
- Named for the Wanapum Indians.[^wiki]
- 2014 spillway crack from a design math error ($61M repair).[^wiki]

# Wenatchee Confluence State Park

![[heading-wenatchee-confluence-state-park.jpg]]
*Photo: Walter Siegmund (talk) — CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Columbia_River_5129.JPG).*

Wenatchee Confluence State Park is a 197-acre park at the north end of Wenatchee where the Wenatchee River meets the Columbia. Established 1990, split by the river into a recreation section and the Horan Natural Area wetland, linked by a footbridge.[^wiki]

Located at the confluence of the Columbia and Wenatchee Rivers, this 194-acre park is a popular destination for year-round camping, cycling and boating. Wenatchee Confluence State Park features a designated swimming area, a wetland nature preserve, grassy sports fields and the longest loop trail in the state runs through the park. A recreational license is required for fishing and shellfish harvesting at Washington State Parks. For regulations, fishing season information, or to purchase a recreational license, visit the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife .[^agency]

## At a glance

- **Managed by:** Washington State Parks

## Natural setting & history

Wenatchee Confluence State Park is a public recreation area and nature preserve at the north end of the city of Wenatchee in Chelan County, Washington. The state park consists of 197 acres (80 ha) spanning the Wenatchee River at its confluence with the Columbia River. The park is bifurcated by the Wenatchee River into north and south sections that are connected by a footbridge. The north section, located in Sunnyslope, is suburban and recreational while the south section, located in West Wenatchee, is a man-made wetland area designated as the Horan Natural Area. The park is operated by the Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission under lease from the Chelan County Public Utility District, which owns the land. Park offerings include camping, boating, fishing, swimming, and various sports activities.

The Apple Capital Recreation Loop Trail runs through the park and connects it to downtown Wenatchee.[^wiki]

Of note:

- At the Wenatchee-Columbia confluence.[^wiki]
- Includes the man-made Horan Natural Area wetland.[^wiki]
- On the Apple Capital Recreation Loop Trail.[^wiki]

# Yakima Sportsman State Park

![[heading-yakima-sportsman-state-park.jpg]]
*Photo: ECTran71 — CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Yakima_Sportsman_State_Park.jpg).*

Yakima Sportsman State Park is a 266-acre park on the Yakima River floodplain on the east side of Yakima (~1,014 ft) — an oasis of green in a desert region — with camping, fishing ponds, and birdwatching. Developed by the Yakima Valley Sportsman's Association and given to the state in 1945.[^wiki]

There is ongoing construction along the Levy Trail. This is a long-term ecosystem restoration project conducted by the federal government and is scheduled until late 2027. The work includes large equipment driving up and down the Levy Trail. Expect extra noise near areas along the Levy Trail and campsites 17 - 36. Yakima Sportsman State Park is a 266-acre camping park originally created by the Yakima Sportsman's Association to promote game management and to preserve our natural resources.[^agency]

## At a glance

- **Managed by:** Washington State Parks
- **Season:** Closed Oct 1–Apr 16
- **Reservations:** Reservable — [Washington State Parks reservations](https://washington.goingtocamp.com)[^resv]
- **Coordinates:** 46.5919, -120.4629
- **Drive from Seattle:** 145 mi · 2 hr 15 min

## Natural setting & history

Yakima Sportsman State Park is a public recreation area located on the Yakima River on the east side of the city of Yakima in Yakima County, Washington. The state park is an oasis of green in an otherwise desert region, encompassing 266 acres (108 ha) of Yakima River floodplain. The site was initially developed by the Yakima Valley Sportsman's Association in the early 1940s, then deeded to the state in 1945. Park offerings include camping, hiking, picnicking, fishing, and birdwatching.[^wiki]

Of note:

- 266 acres on the Yakima River floodplain.[^wiki]
- Developed by the Yakima Valley Sportsman's Association.[^wiki]
- state 1945.[^wiki]
- Known for fishing ponds and birdwatching.[^wiki]
- 104,567 visitors in 2024.[^wiki]

## Plan your visit

Sites are reservable — book through the [reservation system](https://washington.goingtocamp.com)[^resv]. Pets are welcome on leash.

For current conditions, closures and the latest information, see the [official page](https://parks.wa.gov/find-parks/state-parks/yakima-sportsman-state-park)[^official].

## Hazards

- **Weather & winter** — sudden mountain weather & cold nights; hypothermia risk and seasonal road/pass closures. [[Weather & winter]]
- **Wildfire & smoke** — high east-Cascades fire danger, peak Jul–Sep; closures, Red Flag days & wildfire smoke. [[Wildfire & smoke]]
- **Wildlife** — black bear & cougar habitat; secure food, trash and scented items, never feed wildlife. [[Wildlife]]
